questions.q: What is the real point of this capstone, given that it doesn't introduce new Kafka concepts?
options: Proving that the earlier course's decisions — sizing, delivery semantics, error handling — actually compose into one real, working pipeline
Teaching an entirely new API not covered anywhere else in this course
Replacing the need for a consumer group with a simpler pattern
Showing that none of the earlier lessons' choices actually matter in practice
questions.explain: Like every capstone in this catalog, its purpose is proof the earlier material works together, not new material on its own.

questions.q: Why does clickstream-dlq get only 1 partition while the main clickstream topic gets 8?
options: Failures routed to the DLQ should be rare, and unlike the main topic, there's no reason ordering among them needs to be preserved
Kafka requires every dead-letter topic to have exactly 1 partition
1 partition allows for more consumer parallelism than 8 partitions
There is no real reason — the two counts could be swapped with no consequence
questions.explain: The main topic is sized for real throughput and consumer parallelism; the DLQ is sized for its own much smaller, order-independent traffic.

questions.q: Why does this capstone's producer reuse Lesson 25's exact acks=all plus enable.idempotence configuration?
options: Because that combination is still the right call for any producer where losing or duplicating an event is a real problem — a capstone should reuse proven decisions, not invent new ones
Because Kafka requires every producer in a course to use identical settings
Because acks=all and enable.idempotence are deprecated and being phased out
Because the capstone's events cannot be lost or duplicated no matter what the producer is configured to do
questions.explain: The capstone deliberately reuses this course's own established configuration rather than introducing an unrelated new one.

questions.q: How does this pipeline's shape relate to Career & Capstone's Project 3, the streaming fraud detector (Lessons 75-78)?
options: It's the same underlying shape — producer, sized topic, consumer group, dead-letter topic — scoring transactions instead of storing clickstream events
The two systems have no meaningful relationship to each other
Project 3 uses a completely different technology with no relation to Kafka
This capstone is a simplified rewrite of Project 3 with all error handling removed
questions.explain: Both systems ingest real-time events into a sized topic, process them through a consumer group, and need somewhere for a bad event to go instead of blocking everything behind it.

questions.q: Why does the consumer in this capstone call consumer.commit(msg) inside a finally block, regardless of whether processing succeeded?
options: So the offset always advances past the message — whether it processed successfully or got routed to the dead-letter topic — keeping the partition moving either way
finally blocks in Python have no actual effect on program execution
So that a failed message gets reprocessed infinitely until it succeeds
Because committing is only meaningful when processing fails
questions.explain: Committing in the finally block, after either a successful process or a DLQ routing, is what keeps the pipeline from stalling on a message it can't handle.
